title: The data
text:
%pip install openpyxl xlrd


import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import os, json

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression


iwpc = pd.read_excel("../data/IWPC_Data.xls", sheet_name="Subject Data")
meta = pd.read_excel("../data/IWPC_Data.xls", sheet_name="Metadata")
iwpc.shape

5,700 patients from the International Warfarin Pharmacogenetics Consortium. One row per patient; 68 columns. Three things to notice: age is stored as a text range, the genotypes are categorical, and there are missing values throughout.

iwpc.head()
list(iwpc.columns)
meta.head(20)


dose = iwpc["Therapeutic Dose of Warfarin"].dropna()
dose.describe()


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))
axes[0].hist(dose, bins=50);          axes[0].set_title("dose (mg/week)")
axes[1].hist(np.sqrt(dose), bins=50); axes[1].set_title("√dose")
axes[2].hist(np.log(dose), bins=50);  axes[2].set_title("log(dose)")
plt.show()

print("skew, dose: ", dose.skew())
print("skew, √dose:", np.sqrt(dose).skew())
print("skew, log:  ", np.log(dose).skew())


Filtering patients
Two columns decide who is usable. Neither can be a feature — both are known only after treatment — but they can select rows:

Reached a stable dose. If a patient never settled, their recorded dose is not a trustworthy target.
Dose actually recorded. No \(y\), nothing to learn from.

\[5700 \;\xrightarrow{\text{both filters}}\; 5410
      \;\xrightarrow{\text{drop 39 missing ages (next cell)}}\; 5371\]

stable   = iwpc["Subject Reached Stable Dose of Warfarin"] == 1
has_dose = iwpc["Therapeutic Dose of Warfarin"].notna()
keep     = stable & has_dose

iwpc_clean = iwpc[keep]
iwpc_clean.shape


### What needs cleaning
Before encoding anything, check two things for every candidate feature:
how much is missing, and what values the categorical columns actually take.


cols = ["Age", "Height (cm)", "Weight (kg)",
        "VKORC1 -1639 consensus", "CYP2C9 consensus", "Race (OMB)",
        "Carbamazepine (Tegretol)", "Phenytoin (Dilantin)",
        "Rifampin or Rifampicin", "Amiodarone (Cordarone)"]

iwpc_clean[cols].isna().sum()

for c in ["VKORC1 -1639 consensus", "CYP2C9 consensus", "Race (OMB)"]:
    print(iwpc_clean[c].value_counts(dropna=False), "\n")

for c in ["Carbamazepine (Tegretol)", "Phenytoin (Dilantin)",
          "Rifampin or Rifampicin", "Amiodarone (Cordarone)"]:
    print(iwpc_clean[c].value_counts(dropna=False), "\n")    


# Step 3: drop patients with no age (only 39)
data = iwpc_clean.dropna(subset=["Age"]).copy()

# Age: "60 - 69" -> 6   (first character = the decade)
data["age_decades"] = pd.to_numeric(data["Age"].str[0])

# VKORC1: reference = G/G; missing -> "Unknown"
vk = data["VKORC1 -1639 consensus"].fillna("Unknown")
data["vkorc1_AG"]      = (vk == "A/G").astype(int)
data["vkorc1_AA"]      = (vk == "A/A").astype(int)
data["vkorc1_unknown"] = (vk == "Unknown").astype(int)

# CYP2C9: reference = *1/*1; missing or rare alleles -> unknown
cyp = data["CYP2C9 consensus"]
cyp_map = {"*1/*2": "cyp_12", "*1/*3": "cyp_13", "*2/*2": "cyp_22",
           "*2/*3": "cyp_23", "*3/*3": "cyp_33"}
for genotype, name in cyp_map.items():
    data[name] = (cyp == genotype).astype(int)
data["cyp_unknown"] = (~cyp.isin(list(cyp_map) + ["*1/*1"])).astype(int)

# Race: reference = White
race = data["Race (OMB)"]
data["race_asian"]   = (race == "Asian").astype(int)
data["race_black"]   = (race == "Black or African American").astype(int)
data["race_unknown"] = (race == "Unknown").astype(int)


inducers = ["Carbamazepine (Tegretol)", "Phenytoin (Dilantin)", "Rifampin or Rifampicin"]
data["enzyme_inducer"] = (data[inducers].fillna(0) == 1).any(axis=1).astype(int)
data["amiodarone"]     = (data["Amiodarone (Cordarone)"].fillna(0) == 1).astype(int)
print(data["enzyme_inducer"].sum(), data["amiodarone"].sum())

54 246



features = ["age_decades", "Height (cm)", "Weight (kg)",
            "vkorc1_AG", "vkorc1_AA", "vkorc1_unknown",
            "cyp_12", "cyp_13", "cyp_22", "cyp_23", "cyp_33", "cyp_unknown",
            "race_asian", "race_black", "race_unknown",
            "enzyme_inducer", "amiodarone"]

X_df = data[features]
y = np.sqrt(data["Therapeutic Dose of Warfarin"]).to_numpy()   # y ∈ ℝⁿ

print(X_df.shape, y.shape)
print(X_df.isna().sum())


X_train_df, X_test_df, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_df, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)

print(X_train_df.shape, X_test_df.shape)



Imputing height and weight
Height is missing for 19% of patients and weight for 5% — too many to drop. Both are filled with the training median.
The median is a learned parameter, not a fixed constant, so it belongs to the training set. Computing it over the test set would let test patients inform each other’s predictions, and would not match deployment: a clinician with one new patient has no test set to average over. The rule for the rest of this notebook is the same every time — learn on train, apply to both.

medians = X_train_df.median()          # computed from TRAINING patients only

X_train_df = X_train_df.fillna(medians)
X_test_df  = X_test_df.fillna(medians)  # test uses the TRAINING medians

print(X_train_df.isna().sum().sum(), X_test_df.isna().sum().sum())   # both should be 0


scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train = scaler.fit_transform(X_train_df)   # learn x̄ and s, then apply
X_test  = scaler.transform(X_test_df)        # apply the SAME x̄ and s

print(X_train.shape, X_test.shape)
print(X_train.mean(axis=0).round(3)[:3], X_train.std(axis=0).round(3)[:3])


n, p = X_train.shape

w      = np.zeros(p)     # w ∈ ℝ¹⁷
b      = 0.0             # scalar
eta    = 0.1
steps  = 2000
losses = []

for t in range(steps):
    y_hat  = X_train @ w + b              # ŷ = Xw + b1    → vector ∈ ℝⁿ
    r      = y_train - y_hat              # r = y − ŷ      → vector ∈ ℝⁿ
    losses.append(np.mean(r**2))          # L = (1/n) rᵀr  → scalar
    grad_w = -(2/n) * (X_train.T @ r)     # −(2/n) Xᵀr     → vector ∈ ℝ¹⁷
    grad_b = -(2/n) * np.sum(r)           # −(2/n) 1ᵀr     → scalar
    w      = w - eta * grad_w             # w ← w − η∇_w L
    b      = b - eta * grad_b             # b ← b − η ∂L/∂b

assert w.shape == (p,), w.shape


# Standardised weights: units are "per standard deviation of that feature".
# Signs are directly interpretable; magnitudes are NOT comparable across
# features with different spreads (see Cell 21). Sorted by influence.
coef = pd.DataFrame({"feature": features, "w_std": w})
coef.sort_values("w_std", key=abs, ascending=False)


plt.plot(losses)
plt.axhline(y_train.var(), color="red", ls="--", label="predicting the mean")
plt.yscale("log")
plt.xlabel("iteration"); plt.ylabel("MSE (√dose scale)"); plt.legend()
plt.show()


lr = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)

print("sklearn w:", lr.coef_.round(3))
print("your w:   ", w.round(3))
print("max difference:", np.abs(lr.coef_ - w).max())
print("sklearn b:", round(lr.intercept_, 3))


# predictions on the √ scale
y_pred_train = X_train @ w + b
y_pred_test  = X_test  @ w + b

mse_train = np.mean((y_train - y_pred_train)**2)
mse_test  = np.mean((y_test  - y_pred_test )**2)
r2_test   = 1 - mse_test / y_test.var()

print(f"train MSE {mse_train:.3f}   test MSE {mse_test:.3f}   test R² {r2_test:.3f}")


dose_true = y_test**2              # mg/week
dose_pred = y_pred_test**2         # mg/week  ← the back-transform

mae  = np.mean(np.abs(dose_true - dose_pred))
pw20 = np.mean(np.abs(dose_true - dose_pred) <= 0.20 * dose_true)

print(f"MAE: {mae:.2f} mg/week")
print(f"within 20% of the true dose: {100*pw20:.1f}% of patients")


import os
os.makedirs("../images", exist_ok=True)

res_sqrt = y_test - y_pred_test            # residuals on the √ scale
res_raw  = dose_true - dose_pred           # residuals in mg/week

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))

ax[0].hist(res_sqrt, bins=40)
ax[0].set_title("A: residuals, √ scale\n(bell-shaped?)")

ax[1].scatter(y_pred_test, res_sqrt, s=5, alpha=0.3)
ax[1].axhline(0, color="red")
ax[1].set_xlabel("predicted √dose"); ax[1].set_ylabel("residual")
ax[1].set_title("B: √ scale\n(even spread?)")

ax[2].scatter(dose_pred, res_raw, s=5, alpha=0.3)
ax[2].axhline(0, color="red")
ax[2].set_xlabel("predicted dose (mg/week)"); ax[2].set_ylabel("residual (mg/week)")
ax[2].set_title("C: raw mg/week scale\n(even spread?)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("../images/residuals.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")   # BEFORE show
plt.show()

print("residual skew, √ scale:", pd.Series(res_sqrt).skew().round(3))
print("residual skew, raw    :", pd.Series(res_raw).skew().round(3))

bins = pd.qcut(y_pred_test, 4)
print(pd.Series(res_sqrt).groupby(bins).std().round(3))
print(pd.Series(res_raw ).groupby(bins).std().round(2))


w_raw = w / scaler.scale_
b_raw = b - np.sum(w_raw * scaler.mean_)

for name, wr in zip(features, w_raw):
    print(f"{name:20s} {wr:+.4f}")
print(f"{'intercept':20s} {b_raw:+.4f}")


X_test_raw = X_test_df.to_numpy()
print("max difference:", np.abs((X_test_raw @ w_raw + b_raw) - y_pred_test).max())


# ---- Export the trained model -------------------------------------------
# A trained model is just these numbers: 17 weights, one bias, and the feature
# order they belong to. Saved to disk so the website can use them without
# re-running this notebook, and so they never get hand-copied out of date.

model = {
    "features": features,
    "w_raw":    [round(float(v), 6) for v in w_raw],   # float() — np.float64 is not JSON-serialisable
    "b_raw":    round(float(b_raw), 6),

    # sensible starting values for the prediction form
    "defaults": {
        "age_decades": float(X_train_df["age_decades"].median()),
        "height_cm":   float(X_train_df["Height (cm)"].median()),
        "weight_kg":   float(X_train_df["Weight (kg)"].median()),
    },

    # 1st–99th percentile of the training data; outside this the page warns
    # the visitor that the model is extrapolating
    "ranges": {
        "age_decades": [float(X_train_df["age_decades"].min()),
                        float(X_train_df["age_decades"].max())],
        "height_cm":   [float(X_train_df["Height (cm)"].quantile(0.01)),
                        float(X_train_df["Height (cm)"].quantile(0.99))],
        "weight_kg":   [float(X_train_df["Weight (kg)"].quantile(0.01)),
                        float(X_train_df["Weight (kg)"].quantile(0.99))],
    },

    # quoted on the page next to the prediction, so they cannot drift
    "metrics": {
        "n_train":     int(len(y_train)),
        "n_test":      int(len(y_test)),
        "r2_test":     round(float(r2_test), 3),
        "mae_mg_week": round(float(mae), 2),
        "pw20":        round(float(100 * pw20), 1),
        "train_mse":   round(float(mse_train), 3),
        "test_mse":    round(float(mse_test), 3),
    },

    # model card: what this was trained on and how
    "provenance": {
        "data":          "IWPC_Data.xls, 'Subject Data' sheet (ClinPGx downloads)",
        "n_total":       int(len(y)),
        "filters":       "reached stable dose; dose recorded; age recorded",
        "target":        "sqrt(dose in mg/week)",
        "test_size":     0.2,
        "random_state":  0,
        "imputation":    "training median for height and weight",
        "optimizer":     "full-batch gradient descent, eta=0.1, 2000 steps",
        "trained_on":    pd.Timestamp.today().strftime("%Y-%m-%d"),
        "not_for_clinical_use": True,
    },
}

os.makedirs("../model", exist_ok=True)
with open("../model/warfarin_model.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(model, f, indent=2)          # dump → file;  dumps → string

print(f"saved {len(model['w_raw'])} weights to ../model/warfarin_model.json")
print(json.dumps(model["metrics"], indent=2))

title: The Complete Concept Map
text: Machine learning terms get confusing because they belong to different kinds of categories that are usually listed together. This page sorts them. The colors show what kind of thing each idea is:

title: The Complete Concept Map
text:
Map 1: The paradigms
The top of the tree: what your training data looks like. Dashed lines mark hybrids that borrow from two paradigms.






%%{init: {"flowchart": {"wrappingWidth": 280}}}%%
flowchart TB
  ML(["Machine learning"])
  ML --> SUP["<b>Supervised</b><br/>inputs + answers"]
  ML --> UNS["<b>Unsupervised</b><br/>inputs only"]
  ML --> RL["<b>Reinforcement</b><br/>actions + rewards"]
  SUP -.-> WEAK["<b>Weakly supervised</b><br/>coarse or noisy answers"]
  SUP -.-> SEMI["<b>Semi-supervised</b><br/>few answers + many unlabeled"]
  UNS -.-> SEMI
  SUP -.-> SELF["<b>Self-supervised</b><br/>answers made from the input itself"]
  UNS -.-> SELF

  classDef paradigm fill:#FDE2E0,stroke:#C0392B,stroke-width:2px,color:#2C2C2A
  classDef hybrid fill:#FCEBD9,stroke:#D35400,stroke-width:2px,stroke-dasharray:6 4,color:#2C2C2A

  class SUP,UNS,RL paradigm
  class SEMI,SELF,WEAK hybrid

title: The Complete Concept Map
text:
Map 2: Supervised learning: tasks → methods
Blue = the kind of answer you want. Green = model families that can produce it. Many families appear under several tasks: they are tools, not categories.






%%{init: {"flowchart": {"wrappingWidth": 280}}}%%
flowchart TB
  SUP["<b>Supervised</b>"]
  SUP --> REG["<b>Regression</b><br/>y is a number<br/><i>disease progression</i>"]
  SUP --> CLS["<b>Classification</b><br/>y is a category<br/>binary · multiclass · multilabel<br/><i>tumor malignancy, cell type</i>"]
  SUP --> SURV["<b>Time-to-event</b><br/>time until something happens<br/><i>time to relapse</i>"]
  SUP --> SEQL["<b>Per-position labeling</b><br/>a label at every position<br/><i>exon vs intron at each base</i>"]
  SUP --> STRP["<b>Structured prediction</b><br/>a whole object as output<br/><i>3D protein structure</i>"]
  REG --> MREG["linear regression<br/>k-nearest neighbors<br/>support vector regression<br/>Gaussian processes<br/>trees · random forest · boosting<br/>neural networks"]
  CLS --> MCLS["logistic regression<br/>naive Bayes<br/>k-nearest neighbors<br/>support vector machines<br/>trees · random forest · boosting<br/>neural networks"]
  SURV --> MSURV["Cox proportional hazards<br/>random survival forests<br/>neural survival models"]
  SEQL --> MSEQ["hidden Markov models<br/>RNNs / LSTMs<br/>transformers"]
  STRP --> MSTR["transformers + geometry modules<br/><i>AlphaFold</i>"]

  classDef paradigm fill:#FDE2E0,stroke:#C0392B,stroke-width:2px,color:#2C2C2A

Map 3: Unsupervised learning: tasks → methods






%%{init: {"flowchart": {"wrappingWidth": 280}}}%%
flowchart TB
  UNS["<b>Unsupervised</b>"]
  UNS --> CLU["<b>Clustering</b><br/>find groups<br/><i>cell types, strains</i>"]
  UNS --> DRD["<b>Dimensionality reduction</b><br/>few axes that keep the variation<br/><i>20,000 genes → 2–50 axes</i>"]
  UNS --> DEN["<b>Density estimation & generative</b><br/>model the data, make new samples<br/><i>denoise sequencing data</i>"]
  UNS --> ANO["<b>Anomaly detection</b><br/>find the odd samples<br/><i>contaminated runs, rare cells</i>"]
  CLU --> MCLU["k-means<br/>hierarchical clustering<br/>Gaussian mixture models<br/>DBSCAN<br/>Leiden / Louvain <i>(single-cell)</i>"]
  DRD --> MDRD["PCA <i>(linear)</i><br/>NMF · ICA · factor analysis<br/>t-SNE · UMAP <i>(nonlinear, visualization)</i><br/>autoencoders"]
  DEN --> MDEN["kernel density estimation<br/>Gaussian mixture models<br/>hidden Markov models<br/>VAEs <i>(scVI)</i><br/>diffusion models · GANs"]
  ANO --> MANO["isolation forest<br/>autoencoder reconstruction error<br/>distance from cluster centers"]

  class MCLU,MDRD,MDEN,MANO method












Note



PCA is in two places on this site. Here it is a standalone method (explore your data). In the pipeline map below, it is also a preprocessing step inside a bigger model, e.g. normalize → PCA → cluster in single-cell analysis.

title: About
text: About this site

title: Predicting a warfarin dose
text:
ImportantNot medical advice



This page reproduces a published research algorithm as a learning exercise. The predictions here must not be used to dose any real patient. Warfarin dosing is done by clinicians using INR monitoring.

title: Predicting a warfarin dose
text:
1. The problem
Warfarin is a blood thinner given to people at risk of dangerous clots — atrial fibrillation, mechanical heart valves, or a history of deep-vein thrombosis. It has been prescribed tens of millions of times a year.
It is also hard to dose. Too little and the patient can throw a clot and have a stroke. Too much and they can bleed. The dose that keeps a patient in the safe range varies 10- to 20-fold between individuals, and the usual approach is to start everyone near a standard dose and adjust over several weeks using a blood test called the INR (international normalised ratio), which measures how slowly the blood clots. Those first weeks, before the dose settles, are the dangerous period.
The machine learning question: can we predict a patient’s stable dose on day one, from information a doctor already has?
Two genes make this a pharmacogenetics problem rather than a purely clinical one:

CYP2C9 is the liver enzyme that breaks warfarin down. Slower variants mean the drug lingers, so less is needed.
VKORC1 is the protein that warfarin blocks. Some variants produce less of it, so there is less to block, and again less drug is needed.

title: Predicting a warfarin dose
text:
2. The data
The International Warfarin Pharmacogenetics Consortium (IWPC) pooled clinical and genetic data on 5,700 patients from 21 research groups across 9 countries, all of whom had been on warfarin long enough to reach a stable dose. The dataset is distributed through ClinPGx (formerly PharmGKB) and accompanies the 2009 paper Estimation of the warfarin dose with clinical and pharmacogenetic data (PMID: 19228618).
One sample = one patient. The raw table has 68 columns. Most are not usable as model inputs, and sorting them was the first real decision.

What counts as an input
The governing rule in any supervised problem:

A feature is only allowed if you would know it at the moment you need the prediction.

Here that moment is a doctor about to start a patient on warfarin for the first time. Anything measured afterwards is leakage — it makes the model look excellent in testing and useless in practice.








Bucket
Columns
Why




Target (y)
Therapeutic dose of warfarin (mg/week)
what we predict


Allowed inputs
age, height, weight, race, genotypes, interacting drugs, target INR
known before the first dose


Leakage
INR on the reported therapeutic dose
measured after treatment started


Filter
“Subject reached stable dose”
known only afterwards, so it cannot be an input — but it decides which patients have a trustworthy y


Bookkeeping
IDs, project site, free-text comments, raw and QC genotype columns
not information about the patient’s biology



Note that target INR is not leakage, even though it contains the letters INR. The doctor chooses the target before treatment begins — usually 2–3, higher for a mechanical valve. Same acronym, different point in time.
The genotype columns appear three times each — the original lab call, a quality-control recheck, and a reconciled consensus value. Only the consensus columns are used; the others would feed the model the same information two or three times.


Filtering
Keeping only patients who reached a stable dose and have that dose recorded:
\[5700 \;\longrightarrow\; 5410 \;\longrightarrow\; 5371\]
(the second step drops 39 patients with no recorded age). Final dataset: n = 5,371 patients, p = 17 features.

  A linear neuron: weighted sum, bias, identity activation. The back-transform is the only non-linear step.

Using \(n\) for patients and \(p = 17\) for features:








Object
Meaning
Type




\(X\)
data matrix — one row per patient, one column per feature
matrix, \(n \times p\)


\(\mathbf{w}\)
one weight per feature

For a single patient \(i\) (a scalar equation):
\[\hat y_i = \sum_{j=1}^{p} w_j x_{ij} + b = \mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_i + b\]
For every patient at once (a vector equation):
\[\hat{\mathbf{y}} = X\mathbf{w} + b\mathbf{1} \qquad\text{shape check: } (n\times p)(p \times 1) + (n \times 1) \to (n \times 1)\ \checkmark\]
where \(\mathbf{1} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\) is the all-ones vector, so \(b\mathbf{1}\) adds the same bias to every patient.
Weights live on the input wires, not on the patients. Ten thousand more patients would not add a single weight; one more feature would.

title: Predicting a warfarin dose
section: 5. The loss, and why the target is square-rooted
text:
5. The loss, and why the target is square-rooted

Why squared error
\[\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}, \qquad L(\mathbf{w}, b) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i^2 = \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{r}^{\top}\mathbf{r} \quad \text{(a scalar)}\]
MSE is not an arbitrary scoring rule. Suppose the data were generated by the line plus random noise:
\[y_i = \mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_i + b + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) \text{ independently}\]
Then the probability of observing the data we actually observed is
\[\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w},b) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{r_i^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]
Taking logs turns the product into a sum, and the constants drop out because they contain no \(\mathbf{w}\) or \(b\):
\[\log\mathcal{L} = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) \;-\; \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\arg\max_{\mathbf{w},b} \log\mathcal{L} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w},b} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i^2\]
Minimising MSE is maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise of equal spread. Choosing MSE is therefore a claim about the data: errors are bell-shaped, equally spread across patients, and independent. A different claim gives a different loss — heavy-tailed noise gives MAE, a binary outcome gives cross-entropy, count data gives a Poisson loss. The general recipe is \(\text{loss} = -\log(\text{likelihood})\).


Why \(\sqrt{\text{dose}}\)
Raw weekly doses are strongly right-skewed: the middle half of patients sit between 19.5 and 38.5 mg/week, but the maximum is 315.



Target
Skewness




dose
2.36


√dose
0.60


log(dose)
−0.40



Both transforms remove most of the skew; log slightly overcorrects into a left tail. √dose was chosen to match the published model so the coefficients can be compared directly.
Two things follow from the Gaussian story above. Because MSE squares errors, a single patient missed by 140 mg/week contributes as much as about two thousand patients missed by 3 — a long tail in the errors would dominate training. And because biological effects often act multiplicatively, high-dose patients vary more in absolute terms, breaking the equal-spread assumption. Shrinking the scale reduces both problems.
This reasoning is a prediction about the residuals, and §7 tests it.

title: Predicting a warfarin dose
text:
6. Training

The gradient
Differentiating the loss with respect to one weight \(w_j\), holding the others fixed:
\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_j}
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} 2\big(y_i - \textstyle\sum_k w_k x_{ik} - b\big)(-x_{ij})
= -\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{ij} r_i
= -\frac{2}{n}\,\mathbf{x}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\mathbf{r}\]
by the chain rule: the outer square gives \(2(\cdot)\), and the only term inside containing \(w_j\) is \(-w_j x_{ij}\), whose derivative is \(-x_{ij}\). The sum \(\sum_i x_{ij} r_i\) is the dot product of column \(j\) of \(X\) with the residual vector.
Stacking all \(p\) of these gives the gradient, and the stack is exactly a matrix-vector product:
\[\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L =
\begin{bmatrix} -\frac{2}{n}\mathbf{x}_{\cdot 1}^{\top}\mathbf{r} \\ \vdots \\ -\frac{2}{n}\mathbf{x}_{\cdot p}^{\top}\mathbf{r}\end{bmatrix}
= -\frac{2}{n} X^{\top}\mathbf{r}
\qquad (p \times n)(n \times 1) = (p \times 1)\ \checkmark\]
\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = -\frac{2}{n}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{r} \quad \text{(a scalar)}\]
The loss is scalar-valued, so its derivative is a gradient (one entry per unknown), not a Jacobian. The update:
\[\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\,\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L, \qquad b \leftarrow b - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}\]


The code
Each line is one line of the maths above.
n, p   = X_train.shape
w      = np.zeros(p)     # w ∈ ℝ¹⁷
b      = 0.0             # scalar
eta    = 0.1
losses = []

for t in range(2000):
    y_hat  = X_train @ w + b             # ŷ = Xw + b1     → ℝⁿ
    r      = y_train - y_hat             # r = y − ŷ       → ℝⁿ
    losses.append(np.mean(r**2))         # L = (1/n) rᵀr   → scalar
    grad_w = -(2/n) * (X_train.T @ r)    # −(2/n) Xᵀr      → ℝ¹⁷
    grad_b = -(2/n) * np.sum(r)          # −(2/n) 1ᵀr      → scalar
    w      = w - eta * grad_w
    b      = b - eta * grad_b


Does it find the right answer?
Gradient descent is an iterative approximation; the normal equation solves the same problem exactly. Comparing against sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression, which does the latter:
\[\max_j \left| w_j^{\text{GD}} - w_j^{\text{closed form}} \right| = 7.4 \times 10^{-15}\]
Machine precision. The hand-written loop converged to the exact least-squares solution.
Two sanity checks on the training run. At iteration 0, \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}\) and \(b = 0\), so every prediction is zero, \(\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y}\), and the loss should equal \(\overline{y^2} = 5.394^2 + 1.998 = 31.09\) — which is what it printed. And the fitted bias, 5.394, equals the mean of \(\mathbf{y}\), as it must when every feature has been centred.

title: Predicting a warfarin dose
text:
7. Results
All numbers below come from the 1,075 held-out test patients, who were untouched during training, imputation and scaling.





Metric
Value




Test MAE
8.89 mg/week


Within 20% of true dose
45.1%


Test \(R^2\)
0.432


Train MSE (√ scale)
1.097


Test MSE (√ scale)
1.103





Train and test error are nearly identical, so the model is not overfitting at all — unsurprising with 17 weights and 4,296 patients. Its limitation is bias, not variance: too simple to capture everything, rather than too flexible. That is also why regularisation would not help here, and why the honest next step is more features or a non-linear model.
\(R^2 = 0.432\) means genetics and clinical variables explain about 43% of the variation in dose. The other 57% is diet (vitamin K intake), adherence, other medications, unmeasured genetic variants and measurement noise.



Testing the Gaussian assumption
§5 claimed the √ transform would make the residuals more bell-shaped and more evenly spread. Checking it after fitting:




residual skew




√ scale
0.245


raw mg/week
1.222









Figure 1: Residuals on the held-out test patients. A: the error distribution on the √ scale is close to a symmetric bell. B: on the same scale, the spread is roughly even across the range of predictions. C: in raw mg/week, the spread fans out badly with dose — the unequal variance that MSE assumes away.



On the √ scale the residuals form a near-symmetric bell centred on zero. On the raw mg/week scale they are visibly right-skewed, and the residual-versus-prediction plot fans out: errors around a predicted 15 mg/week span roughly ±20, while errors around a predicted 50 span −30 to +60. That funnel is precisely the unequal spread that MSE assumes away.
So the transform decision is verified rather than assumed — a decision made for a stated reason, then tested against the data.

title: Predicting a warfarin dose
text:
8. Comparison with the published algorithm
Converting the trained weights out of standardised units. If \(\tilde x_{ij} = (x_{ij} - \bar x_j)/s_j\), then substituting into \(\hat y_i = \sum_j \tilde w_j \tilde x_{ij} + \tilde b\) and separating the patient-dependent terms gives
\[w_j = \frac{\tilde w_j}{s_j}, \qquad b = \tilde b - \sum_{j=1}^{p} w_j \bar x_j\]
Nothing about the model changes — the same predictions, re-expressed in years, centimetres and kilograms.
The resulting equation (output is √dose in mg/week; every indicator is 0 or 1; the reference patient is White, VKORC1 G/G, CYP2C9 *1/*1, on no interacting drugs):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{\text{dose}} = \;& 5.483 \\
&- 0.2390 \times \text{age in decades} \\
&+ 0.00847 \times \text{height (cm)} \;+\; 0.01339 \times \text{weight (kg)} \\
&- 0.8403 \times \text{VKORC1 A/G} \;-\; 1.5895 \times \text{VKORC1 A/A} \;-\; 0.6567 \times \text{VKORC1 unknown} \\
&- 0.4783 \times \text{CYP2C9 *1/*2} \;-\; 0.8906 \times \text{*1/*3} \;-\; 1.1489 \times \text{*2/*2} \\
&\qquad - 1.8309 \times \text{*2/*3} \;-\; 2.1401 \times \text{*3/*3} \;-\; 0.4026 \times \text{CYP2C9 unknown} \\
&- 0.3139 \times \text{Asian} \;-\; 0.1097 \times \text{Black or African American} \;-\; 0.1656 \times \text{race unknown} \\
&+ 1.0554 \times \text{enzyme inducer} \;-\; 0.6221 \times \text{amiodarone}
\end{aligned}
\]
Two structures fall out of the fitted numbers that nobody put in:
The CYP2C9 coefficients order themselves by enzyme impairment. *1/*2 (−0.48) → *1/*3 (−0.89) → *2/*2 (−1.15) → *2/*3 (−1.83) → *3/*3 (−2.14). The *3 allele impairs the enzyme more than *2, and two impaired copies more than one. The model was given six unrelated 0/1 columns and recovered that ordering from the data alone.
VKORC1 is additive. \(-1.589 \approx 2 \times (-0.840)\): two copies of the A allele lower the dose about twice as much as one. This is testable only because each genotype was given its own free weight — an allele-count encoding would have assumed it.
Every coefficient sign matches the pharmacology: older patients need less, bigger patients need more, impaired metabolism needs less, enzyme inducers need more, amiodarone (a CYP2C9 inhibitor) needs less.

Things worth trying: switch VKORC1 from G/G to A/A and watch the dose roughly halve — that single gene is the strongest predictor in the model. Set CYP2C9 to *3/*3 as well and the predicted dose collapses, which is exactly the patient most at risk of bleeding on a standard starting dose. Then set both genotypes to “not genotyped” and see the model hedge back toward the middle.

title: Predicting a warfarin dose
text:
10. Limitations
It is not clinically usable. Beyond being a reproduction, the model predicts a stable dose; real dosing also requires a loading strategy and INR monitoring.
It explains 43% of the variation. More than half of what determines a warfarin dose is not in this dataset — vitamin K intake, adherence, liver function, other drugs, and genetic variants that were not measured.
Race is used as a feature, and that deserves scrutiny. It is included here because the published algorithm includes it, and it carries real predictive signal. But race is a social category standing in, imperfectly, for genetic ancestry and for environmental factors. The consequence is that model accuracy differs across populations, and the IWPC cohort was predominantly White and Asian. A later follow-up found a variant (rs12777823) that substantially improved dose prediction in African-American patients and is not in this model at all. A better version would use measured ancestry or additional variants instead of a race checkbox; comparing a model with and without the race terms is a natural next experiment.
Two coefficients rest on very few patients. Only about 55 of 5,371 patients were on an enzyme inducer (carbamazepine 27, phenytoin 24, rifampin 4), so the +1.06 inducer weight is imprecise. The same applies to CYP2C9 *3/*3 (19 patients).
The medication fields were assumed, not observed. About 57% of medication entries were blank and were treated as “not taking”. If instead some sites simply never recorded these fields, that assumption is wrong for those patients.
Missing genotypes were given their own category. The “unknown” weight is not biology; it is the average effect among patients whose genotype was not recorded, and it may also absorb differences between the sites that did and did not genotype.
The test set measures one split. A single 80/20 split with a fixed seed gives one estimate; cross-validation would give a confidence interval around it.
